guidance.procedure: After deciding the relation, collect every complete responsive member: the operative sentence plus any governing lead-in, definition introduction, exception introduction, or continuation needed to express its force, actor, object, trigger, or scope. Include repeated provisions that independently resolve the hypothesis. Exclude headings, neighboring examples, generic security or duration language, and clauses that are merely useful context.

operations.rationale: Across the batch, most correct relations still omitted governing introductions, continuations, or repeated operative provisions, while several answers copied nearby but nonresponsive clauses.

guidance.procedure: Inspect the disclosure prohibition together with its exceptions and the identity of permitted recipients. A pattern such as “do not disclose except to necessary agents, consultants, or advisers” supports sharing some information with some third parties. A ban followed only by access for the recipient’s employees or officers opposes third-party sharing; a bare ban with no responsive exception also opposes it. Do not treat employees alone as third parties.

operations.rationale: The lawyer repeatedly reversed this relation by focusing on the prohibition while ignoring a third-party exception, or by treating employee-only access as permission for outside recipients.

guidance.procedure: Evaluate possession after the required return or destruction is completed. An express archival, backup, legal, dispute, or other retention exception supports permissible post-return possession. A requirement to return or destroy all information or copies, with no retention carve-out, opposes it; choosing destruction instead of return does not imply that something may remain. A return duty alone does not become permission merely because possession existed before the trigger.

operations.rationale: Several answers inferred retention from return/destruction language itself, although only an express surviving-copy exception supports the hypothesis.

guidance.procedure: Match the return-or-destroy trigger to termination of the agreement or relationship. “Upon termination, return or destroy” supports the hypothesis. “Upon request” or “upon demand” alone does not, even if placed in a return section or even if the agreement can separately terminate; it supports the hypothesis only when the request duty is expressly tied to termination. Do not substitute transaction abandonment or an unrelated trigger without textual linkage.

operations.rationale: The lawyer twice treated request-based return clauses as termination-triggered duties and was distracted by section placement.

guidance.procedure: Look for obligations that expressly continue, survive, remain enforceable, or are not released after termination or expiration. A fixed agreement term, an effective-date duration, or language that the agreement remains in force is not by itself an obligation-survival provision. If the text affirmatively ends the relevant duties at termination or confines them to the agreement term, it opposes survival; otherwise duration language without a post-termination link leaves the hypothesis unresolved.

operations.rationale: The lawyer repeatedly converted ordinary term clauses into survival provisions and included duration clauses that did not independently govern post-termination obligations.

guidance.procedure: Test the word “only” against the operative confidential-information definition or deeming provisions. Express inclusion of business, financial, marketing, personnel, customer, contractual, or similarly nontechnical information contradicts a technical-only definition. A definition expressly confined to technical information supports it. Generic breadth such as “all information” or background discussion of commercial material, without an operative identifiable nontechnical category, does not automatically settle the proposition.

operations.rationale: Errors came from both overreading generic breadth as contradiction and overlooking expressly nontechnical categories; evidence lists were also incomplete.

guidance.procedure: Because the hypothesis concerns all confidential information, verify whether identification or marking is a universal condition, including any oral-information procedure. A clause protecting information whether or not labeled, or protecting information merely because a reasonable person would understand it as confidential, opposes universal express identification. A broad definition with no marking rule is unresolved, not automatically contradictory; cite the complete marking sequence when it is the governing condition.

operations.rationale: The lawyer sometimes inferred identification from confidentiality or nonpublic status, and elsewhere omitted parts of the multi-step marking regime.

guidance.procedure: Require the definition or disclosure rule to cover communication mode. Express references to oral, spoken, verbal, visual, or a comprehensive tangible/intangible disclosure formulation support inclusion of verbally conveyed information. A clause about discussions, agreement content, or information existing “in any form” inside a subject-matter list does not necessarily establish oral disclosure. If the contract addresses content but not conveyance mode, use NotMentioned rather than inference.

operations.rationale: The lawyer missed a comprehensive mode definition and also inferred oral coverage merely from references to discussions.

guidance.procedure: An exclusion or exception for information independently developed without use of or access to protected information supports permissible independent development; include the exception’s governing lead-in as well as the specific limb when both carry its legal force. A nondisclosure, nonuse, or copying prohibition does not prohibit independent development by implication. Without an express development rule or an actual opposing prohibition, the issue is unresolved.

operations.rationale: The lawyer sometimes treated silence or an unrelated disclosure ban as a prohibition and frequently omitted the exception introduction.

guidance.procedure: A definition exclusion or exception for information lawfully received from an unrestricted third-party source supports acquiring similar information from a third party. Include the governing exclusion lead-in and any conditions identifying the lawful, nonconfidential source. A ban on disclosing the current confidential information says nothing about acquiring other information and therefore is not contradiction. Do not infer permission solely from a public-domain or independent-development exception.

operations.rationale: The lawyer confused outgoing disclosure restrictions with incoming acquisition and often cited only the final exception limb, omitting its governing introduction.

guidance.procedure: Distinguish express permission from prohibition. “May copy only as reasonably necessary for the stated purpose” supports permissible copying; “shall not copy” or “shall not copy without prior consent” opposes it. A general right to use information does not itself grant copying, and a general nondisclosure duty does not itself prohibit copying. When the operative copy rule follows a lead-in identifying the recipient’s undertakings, include both if needed for actor and force.

operations.rationale: The lawyer inferred copying permission from use and reversed an express no-copy clause, while often omitting the governing undertaking introduction.

guidance.procedure: Separate permission to comply with law from a duty to notify. Entailment requires language obligating the receiving party to give notice, an opportunity to object, or equivalent warning when disclosure is legally compelled. A compelled-disclosure exception without notice leaves the notice hypothesis unresolved. For evidence, include any governing exception lead-in and the operative notice provision, but exclude a generic legal-disclosure permission unless it is part of that condition.

operations.rationale: Relations were usually correct, but complete evidence was repeatedly missed and generic compelled-disclosure permission was sometimes overincluded.

guidance.procedure: Find an express allowance for disclosure or access to the receiving party’s employees, ordinarily conditioned on need to know or the stated purpose. Such an allowance supports sharing with some employees even when general disclosure is prohibited. Permission only for outside advisers does not establish employee sharing. A bare third-party nondisclosure or no-copy clause, without addressing employees, leaves employee sharing unresolved rather than opposing it.

operations.rationale: The lawyer wrongly treated a general third-party ban as an employee-sharing prohibition and often omitted the clause introducing the recipient’s disclosure obligations.

guidance.procedure: Support limited use with provisions that actually restrict use to the stated purpose or forbid every other use, including a governing purpose clause when it supplies the operative limit. Include repeated independently operative nonuse provisions. Do not cite confidentiality, security, disclosure, copying, survival, or no-license language merely because it is nearby; those provisions are members only if they themselves impose the hypothesis’s use limitation.

operations.rationale: The relation was stable, but every case showed evidence omissions or additions, especially generic confidentiality, duration, and no-license clauses.

guidance.procedure: Treat an express denial of any license, title, right of use, or other interest in the confidential information as support. Property-retention language is responsive only when it independently denies the recipient a right, not merely because it names the owner. Where a sentence begins with a construction formula and continues into a subordinate no-right provision, include the complete linked provision; include separate no-license clauses when each independently resolves the hypothesis.

operations.rationale: Labels were reliable, but evidence repeatedly omitted linked introductory language or a second independently responsive denial of rights.
